title: git status takes eight seconds. Fix it.
summary: On a repository with tens of thousands of files, everyday commands crawl. Measure where the time goes, then turn on the four settings that fix it — none of which change a single commit.
mental_model: `git status` stats every file; history commands walk every commit. The fixes are caches — of untracked-file scans, of filesystem events, and of the commit graph. They are all local, all safe, and all reversible.

setup.run: sh -c 'for d in $(seq 1 12); do mkdir -p src/module$d; for f in $(seq 1 25); do printf "VALUE_%d = %d\n" $f $f > src/module$d/file$f.py; done; done'
sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 40); do printf "# revision %d\n" $i >> src/module1/file1.py; git commit -q -a -m "Change $i"; done'

steps.title: Measure before changing anything
steps.why: Three hundred files and forty-one commits is small, but the mechanics are identical at a hundred times the size. Establish the baseline: how many files git stats, and how many commits it walks.
steps.expect: File and commit counts, and a timing for status.

steps.title: See where the time actually goes
steps.why: `GIT_TRACE_PERFORMANCE=1` prints per-phase timings. On a slow `git status` the dominant line is nearly always the untracked-file scan or the index refresh — knowing which one decides the fix.
steps.expect: Timed phases, including reading the index and scanning the working tree.

steps.title: Cache the untracked-file scan
steps.why: `core.untrackedCache` remembers which directories had untracked files and their mtimes, so status re-scans only directories that actually changed. It is the single biggest win on a large working tree.

steps.title: Write a commit-graph
steps.why: History traversal walks commit objects one at a time. The commit-graph file stores parents and generation numbers in one place, which makes `log --graph`, `merge-base` and `branch --contains` dramatically faster on deep histories.

steps.title: Turn on the bundle of large-repo defaults
steps.why: `feature.manyFiles` is an umbrella that enables the index version and untracked cache settings suited to big trees. One line instead of remembering four.

verify.label: the many-files feature bundle is on

steps.title: Register background maintenance
steps.why: `git maintenance` keeps the commit-graph fresh, repacks incrementally and prefetches — the work that otherwise happens as a surprise ten-second `gc` in the middle of your afternoon.

verify.label: maintenance is configured for this repository

steps.title: Know the one that needs a daemon
steps.why: `core.fsmonitor true` uses the built-in filesystem monitor so git is told which files changed instead of statting all of them. It is the biggest win of all on a huge tree, and the only one here with a background process attached.
commands: sh -c 'git config core.fsmonitor true && echo "fsmonitor enabled"'
sh -c 'git config --unset core.fsmonitor && echo "disabled again for this sandbox"'
steps.expect: It configures cleanly; on a real large repository this is where the seconds disappear.

steps.title: Confirm nothing about the repository changed
steps.why: Every setting above is a cache or a local config. The commits, trees and blobs are identical — which is why these are safe to apply to any repository without asking anyone.

verify.label: the history is untouched — these are caches, not rewrites
a commit-graph speeds up history traversal
no commit was changed by any of it

pitfalls: All of these are per-clone config. Document them in your README, because a colleague's slow git is not fixed by your settings.
`core.fsmonitor true` starts a background daemon. On network filesystems and some container mounts it misbehaves — measure before and after rather than assuming.
A commit-graph goes stale as you commit. `git maintenance` refreshes it; writing it once and forgetting is a common half-fix.
If `git status` is slow because of a huge untracked build directory, the real fix is `.gitignore`. Caching a scan you should not be doing is the wrong layer.
`GIT_TRACE_PERFORMANCE=1` before optimising, and again afterwards. Every recommendation here helps some repositories much more than others.
cheatsheet: let the filesystem tell git what changed
keep the caches fresh in the background
